result.result:
I fixed the duplicate check. Before this change, two rules on the same path with different methods (`GET /` and `POST /`) raised `DuplicateRuleError`, which would break most apps. The full test suite passes (982 tests), including the new tests. I couldn't run ruff or mypy because neither is installed in `.venv`. Nothing is committed.

## The fix

**Methods.** The duplicate check is now its own method, `Rule._is_duplicate(other)` in `src/werkzeug/routing/rules.py`, and `matcher.py` calls it instead of `==`. Two rules are duplicates when all of these hold:
- They have the same parts, meaning the same path and subdomain or host, with variable parts counted as equal only if they use the same converter.
- They have the same websocket mode.
- They share at least one method. A rule with `methods=None` accepts any method, so it overlaps with every other rule on that path.
- `HEAD` counts as shared, because it's added automatically whenever `GET` is present. So `["GET"]` and `["HEAD"]` are duplicates.

**One case you should check: `OPTIONS`.** A plain intersection would break Flask. Flask adds `OPTIONS` to every rule automatically, so `@app.get("/")` and `@app.post("/")` would share `{"OPTIONS"}` and raise. So if the only shared method is `OPTIONS`, I don't count it as a duplicate, unless one of the rules handles *only* `OPTIONS`. That rule could never be reached, so it is a real duplicate.

**`__eq__`.** I put it back to the 3.1 behaviour, `self._trace == other._trace`, because `==` is still used elsewhere (`provides_defaults_for` uses `self != rule`). #3038 had changed that meaning; since 3.2 isn't released yet, reverting it breaks no one.

**`strict_slashes` and `merge_slashes`.**
- `merge_slashes` was already handled. The rule's slashes are merged before its parts are built, so `/a//b` is a duplicate of `/a/b` when merging is on, and a different rule when the map or the rule turns merging off.
- `strict_slashes` doesn't need to be part of the check. `/a` and `/a/` always produce different parts, and when both exist each one matches its own URL. `strict_slashes` only decides whether a missing trailing slash gets a redirect when there's no `/a` rule.

**Tests** (`tests/test_routing.py`): disjoint methods, shared methods (including the `HEAD`, `None` and `OPTIONS` cases), websocket combined with methods, leaf vs. branch under both `strict_slashes` settings, `merge_slashes` on and off at map and rule level, and `==` staying separate from the duplicate check. I also updated `docs/routing.rst` and the `CHANGES.rst` entry.

## Why `Rule.methods` can be `None`

`None` means the rule accepts **any** method. That's documented on the `methods` parameter but easy to miss. Werkzeug itself never defaults to `GET`; that default comes from Flask, which always passes a list. Werkzeug can't use a fixed set for "any method" because methods are open-ended, including custom ones, so the `None` checks throughout the code are how "any method" is handled. I made this explicit in the `methods` docstring.

## Separate bug, not fixed here

The slash-merging regex `"/{2,}?"` is non-greedy, so `///a` becomes `//a` instead of `/a`. It's used both when building a rule and when matching a request, so the two stay consistent. It's still wrong, but it's outside this issue.
